h1: The 8 Best Rice Cookers Under $200 of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Rice Cooker Under $200 2026: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: the 8 best rice cookers under $200, from Zojirushi Micom models to AROMA multicookers that cost a fraction as much.
summary: The Zojirushi NS-TSC18 is the best rice cooker under $200: Micom fuzzy-logic control at 1.8 liters, with a warmer. The NS-TPC10XT swaps size for a PFAS-free pot, and the 3-cup Micom suits small kitchens. For a tighter budget, the AROMA cookers add steam, slow-cook and oatmeal modes at $25 to $50.
intro: Rice cookers fall into two camps, and the price tag hides which one you are buying. A basic cooker has one heating element and a thermostat that trips when the water is gone. A Micom model carries a small computer that adjusts heat through the cycle, which is why it copes with brown rice, sushi rice and half batches without scorching the bottom.

We ranked eight cookers under $200 from their listings, scoring them on the Primea framework: control type, capacity, pot material, extra modes and price bracket. Micom control carried the most weight, so the list opens with it and works down to plain cookers. The mistake worth avoiding is buying the biggest pot when you cook for one.

products.name: Zojirushi NS-TSC18 Micom Rice Cooker and Warmer, 1.8 Liters
products.verdict: The largest Micom fuzzy-logic cooker in the lineup, built for families.
products.description:
The NS-TSC18 is a rice cooker and warmer with Micom fuzzy-logic controls and a 1.8 liter pot. The microcomputer is the point: it adjusts heat as the cycle runs, which is how it holds a stable result across rice types and batch sizes where a thermostat cooker simply boils and clicks off.

It ranks first because it puts that control into the largest pot here. The NS-TPC10XT has the same Micom class in a 5.5-cup body, so what separates them is capacity and coating, and the bigger machine serves more households. Both sit in the $100 to $200 bracket.

Buy it if you cook rice most nights for several people. The caveat is footprint: it is the largest machine in the group and takes real counter space, which is wasted on a household of one or two.
products.idealFor: Families that cook rice nearly every day.
products.skipIf: You cook for one or two.

products.name: Zojirushi NS-TPC10XT Micom Rice Cooker & Warmer (with PFAS-Free Nonstick), 5.5-Cup, Stainless Brown
products.verdict: Micom control with a PFAS-free nonstick inner pot.
products.description:
The NS-TPC10XT is the same Micom idea in a 5.5-cup body with a PFAS-free nonstick inner pot and a stainless brown finish, in the $100 to $200 bracket. Rice sticks to a pot's surface, so the coating decides both cleanup and how long the pot lasts.

It ranks second because the coating is the main reason to pick it over the NS-TSC18, which holds more. For a household of three or four, 5.5 cups covers a normal dinner, and you gain a pot free of PFAS chemicals. Among the Micom machines it is the one for buyers who read cookware labels.

Buy it for a mid-size household or anyone avoiding PFAS. The caveat is the smaller pot: if you batch cook for a crowd or meal prep, the NS-TSC18 above it holds more.

products.name: Zojirushi Micom 3-Cup Compact Size Rice Cooker and Warmer, Stainless Steel
products.verdict: Micom control in a 3-cup body with a retractable cord.
products.description:
Zojirushi's 3-cup Micom brings fuzzy-logic control down to a stainless steel body with a built-in retractable power cord, in the $100 to $200 bracket. Micom matters more at small sizes than people expect, since a thermostat cooker tends to scorch a small quantity of rice.

It ranks third because capacity caps at 3 cups, so the larger Micom units serve more people. It beats the basic 3-cup Zojirushi below on control type, even though both cost within a bracket of each other. The cord that tucks away makes it the easiest pick here to store in a dorm or small kitchen.

Buy it if you cook for one or two and want the Micom result. The caveat is price: you pay Micom money for a small pot, so a crowd needs a bigger model.
products.idealFor: Singles and couples in small kitchens.

products.name: Zojirushi 6-Cup Rice Cooker
products.verdict: A 6-cup Zojirushi for buyers who skip Micom sensing.
products.description:
This 6-cup Zojirushi is a plain cooker in the $50 to $100 bracket, with no Micom control listed. It offers the capacity of a family machine, and the listing leans on the brand's build quality instead of features.

It ranks fourth for a simple reason: it undercuts the Micom models on price while keeping the name. A larger household that eats white rice and wants no menu gets exactly that. It trails the AROMA cookers below it on modes, since the listing names no advanced settings, but it is likelier to hold up over years of daily use.

Buy it if you feed four or more and prefer simple controls. Skip it if you cook brown rice or sushi rice regularly, because thermostat-only cooking has no way to adapt the heat to the grain.
products.idealFor: Larger households that prefer simple controls.

products.name: Zojirushi 3 Cup Rice Cooker/Steamer (White)
products.verdict: Zojirushi's compact basic cooker with a steamer function.
products.description:
The 3-cup Zojirushi in white is a rice cooker and steamer combination in the $50 to $100 bracket. Its listing mentions the steamer function and the brand's build quality, but no Micom control.

It lands fifth because it is the same idea as the 6-cup model at half the capacity. Its argument is price against the 3-cup Micom, and it makes that case without convincing: you save money and lose the adaptive heating that makes small batches reliable. Against the AROMA cookers it keeps the brand but not their extra modes.

Buy it if you cook for one or two, want a steamer for vegetables and prefer a simple machine. Skip it if you eat rice weekly and care about texture, since the Micom version a bracket up is the better rice maker.
products.idealFor: One or two people wanting a simple steamer.

products.award: Best for Big Households on a Budget
products.name: AROMA Digital Rice Cooker, 4-Cup (Uncooked) / 8-Cup (Cooked), ARC-914SBD
products.verdict: Digital controls, steamer and grain modes at a budget price.
products.description:
The ARC-914SBD is a 2 quart digital AROMA with 4-cup uncooked and 8-cup cooked capacity, a stainless exterior, and steamer, grain and multicooker functions, all for $25 to $50. The digital panel brings preset programs that a basic cooker cannot offer.

It ranks sixth because it trades Micom sensing for price and range. Digital control is not fuzzy logic: it follows set programs rather than adjusting heat as the rice cooks. Against the Zojirushi 6-cup, it offers far more modes, but the Zojirushi brings the better reputation for build.

Buy it for a bigger household on a small budget that also wants to steam and cook grains. The caveat is the missing fuzzy logic, so rice quality will not match the Micom machines at the top.

products.name: AROMA Digital Rice Cooker, 4-Cup (Uncooked) / 8-Cup (Cooked), 2 Qt, Multicooker
products.verdict: Adds slow-cook and oatmeal modes for a very low cost.
products.description:
This second AROMA is also a 2 quart digital cooker with 4-cup uncooked and 8-cup cooked capacity, steam and multicook modes, and a stainless exterior. What it adds is slow-cook and oatmeal-cook modes, plus an auto keep-warm setting, for $25 to $50.

It ranks seventh, one place below the ARC-914SBD, only because rice is not its main job. Slow cook turns it into a countertop pot for stews, and the oatmeal mode helps on workday mornings. Compared with the Micom Zojirushis, that flexibility is the trade, since those machines concentrate on rice texture.

Buy it if you want a single appliance for rice, oats and slow-cooked dinners. Skip it if perfect rice is the only goal, because there is no fuzzy logic here and the multi-mode design splits attention.
products.idealFor: Cooks wanting one appliance for many uses.
products.skipIf: Perfect rice is your only goal.

products.name: AROMA Rice Cooker, 3-Cup (Uncooked) / 6-Cup (Cooked), ARC-363NG
products.verdict: A 1.5 quart cooker that also makes oatmeal and soup, for under $25.
products.description:
The ARC-363NG is the smallest and cheapest pick: 3 cups uncooked and 6 cups cooked in a 1.5 quart bowl, with auto keep-warm, under $25. It also doubles as an oatmeal cooker and soup maker, which stretches a small budget.

It ranks last because it is the simplest machine in the list, with basic controls and the smallest capacity of the AROMAs. The price gap is wide, though: it costs a fraction of any Zojirushi, and the extra modes cover tasks that a basic cooker would not.

Buy it for a dorm room, a first apartment or a single cook on a minimal budget. Skip it if you feed more than two people, since a 6-cup cooked yield runs out fast and there is no larger pot to scale up.
products.idealFor: Students and singles on a minimal budget.
products.skipIf: You cook for more than two.

whatMatters.detail: Micom stands for microcomputer: the cooker adjusts heat through the cycle instead of heating until a thermostat trips. That helps with brown rice, sushi rice and small batches, which scorch easily on basic cookers. The Zojirushi NS-TSC18, NS-TPC10XT and 3-cup Micom have it. Look for the word Micom in the product title, because a brand name alone does not prove it.

Cup ratings count uncooked rice, and the cooked yield is roughly double. A 3-cup machine feeds one or two people, while 5.5 or 6 cups suits a family. Buying too big wastes counter space and leaves rice sitting warm. Match the number to who you feed, and check whether the listing says uncooked or cooked, since an 8-cup cooked rating means only 4 cups of dry rice.

Rice sticks to the pot, so the coating sets cleanup and wear. Some pots are PFAS-free nonstick, like the one in the Zojirushi NS-TPC10XT. That matters if you prefer to avoid those chemicals in cookware. Check the title or spec list for the coating claim, because most listings are silent on it, and if the claim is absent assume a conventional nonstick pot.

Slow-cook, steam, grain and oatmeal modes turn a rice cooker into a general appliance. They matter if kitchen space is limited, and the AROMA cookers lean on them. The Zojirushi picks here list fewer modes. Read the title and bullet list for the modes by name, and ignore generic words like multifunction, which tell you nothing about what the dial really does.

A keep-warm function holds rice at serving temperature after the cycle. It matters when meals are staggered, since rice left on a bare element dries out and crusts. The Zojirushi NS-TSC18 is a cooker and warmer, and the AROMA ARC-363NG has auto keep-warm. Look for warmer or keep-warm in the listing, and note whether it is automatic or a button you must press yourself.

faq.q: Does every Zojirushi here have Micom?
faq.a: No. The 6-cup and the 3-cup white models list no Micom controls, and they cost less for it. The NS-TSC18, NS-TPC10XT and the 3-cup Micom do. Check the title for the word Micom, since the Zojirushi name alone does not guarantee fuzzy logic.

Buying by price bracket instead of household size, assuming the dearest model must fit best. A 1.8 liter machine like the NS-TSC18 is wasted on one person, who would be better served by the 3-cup Micom or the AROMA ARC-363NG.

faq.q: Is Micom worth it over an AROMA?
faq.a: If rice is a weekly staple, yes: the Zojirushi NS-TSC18 adapts heat across grains and small batches. If you want steam, slow-cook and oatmeal modes cheaply, an AROMA at $25 to $50 is the better value.

faq.q: How do I measure the rice?
faq.a: Use the measuring cup that comes with the cooker, since cooker cups differ from standard US cups, and rinse the grain first. Fill to the matching water line inside the pot, and level the rice before starting the cycle on any model here.

faq.q: How do I clean the pot?
faq.a: Wash the pot by hand with a soft sponge, especially nonstick ones like the NS-TPC10XT, and dry it before use. Avoid metal utensils and abrasive pads, which scratch the surface and shorten its life.

faq.q: Can I cook oatmeal in these?
faq.a: Only the AROMA models list oatmeal: the 2 quart multicooker with slow-cook and oatmeal modes, and the ARC-363NG. The Zojirushi listings here do not, so a daily oatmeal habit points you toward AROMA.

finalTake: For most households, the Zojirushi NS-TSC18 is the rice cooker to buy under $200: Micom control, 1.8 liters and a warmer. Choose the NS-TPC10XT if you want a PFAS-free pot in a smaller body, or the 3-cup Micom for a small kitchen. On a tight budget, the AROMA cookers add steam, slow-cook and oatmeal modes, trading away fuzzy logic.
